title: LIC Shares Plunge 9% as Government Launches Massive 6.5% Stake Sale at Steep Discount
excerpt: India's largest divestment move since LIC's 2022 IPO aims to meet SEBI's public shareholding norms and could raise over ₹31,000 crore.
body:
• Shares of Life Insurance Corporation fell as much as 9.26% on Tuesday after the government announced a stake sale of up to 6.5% at a floor price of ₹382 — an 11% discount to Monday's close of ₹428.50.
  • The offer for sale comprises a base offer of 2% equity, with a greenshoe option to sell an additional 4.5%, making it the government's largest divestment move since LIC's 2022 IPO.
  • A fully subscribed sale would lift LIC's public shareholding to 10%, meeting SEBI's minimum threshold well ahead of the May 2027 deadline.
  • The government has already raised ₹21,200 crore through stake sales this fiscal year; the LIC OFS alone could add another ₹31,400 crore.

Life Insurance Corporation's stock suffered its sharpest single-day fall in months on Tuesday after the government moved to sell up to a 6.5% stake in India's largest insurer through an offer for sale, its first such divestment since LIC listed in May 2022.

The Discount Hit Hard

LIC shares slumped as much as 9.26% to their lowest level in nearly four months, as the floor price of ₹382 per share represented a steep 11% discount to Monday's closing price. The selloff was immediate and broad — institutional investors who had accumulated positions over the past year scrambled to reassess their holdings against the incoming supply.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=kE8jTcGXlUE

The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management announced the OFS on Monday evening, offering a base tranche of 2% equity with the option to sell an additional 4.5% under a greenshoe mechanism if demand warrants. Non-retail investors bid on Tuesday, with the retail window opening Wednesday.

Why Now?

The timing raised eyebrows. LIC still had roughly 10 months to meet the Securities and Exchange Board of India's minimum 10% public shareholding requirement — a deadline originally set for May 2027. Market analyst Ambareesh Baliga called the timing "curious," questioning whether divestment funds were being redirected to plug the oil import deficit or fund capital expenditure.

"The question which comes up is whether the divestment funds are being diverted to fund the oil deficit or whether it's going for capex."

— Ambareesh Baliga, Mumbai-based market analyst

The government has set an ambitious ₹80,000 crore ($8.39 billion) divestment target for the current fiscal year. The LIC sale alone could contribute roughly ₹31,400 crore if the full greenshoe is exercised — nearly 40% of the annual goal in a single transaction.

Structural Upside, Short-Term Pain

Analysts conceded the near-term pressure was real but noted the structural benefits. "The increase in public shareholding is structurally positive because it improves liquidity and institutional accessibility," said Ajit Mishra, senior vice president of research at Religare Broking. Greater free float makes LIC more attractive to foreign institutional investors and could eventually support index inclusion upgrades.

LIC has underperformed the broader market this year, falling 7.83% against the Nifty 50's 6.37% decline. The median analyst target still rates the stock a "buy" according to LSEG data, suggesting the selloff may be creating an entry point for long-term investors.

Divestment Machine in Full Gear

The LIC OFS is the latest in a busy year of government stake sales. India has already divested holdings in Coal India, NHPC, GIC Re, Central Bank of India, NLC India, and IRFC, raising about ₹21,200 crore. The LIC transaction signals that New Delhi is prepared to use its blue-chip public sector holdings aggressively to meet fiscal targets — a pattern that NRI investors in Indian PSU stocks should monitor closely.

By mid-afternoon in Mumbai, LIC shares were trading around ₹395, down roughly 8% on the day.
nri_angle: LIC is India's most widely held insurance company with over 280 million policies; NRI investors who bought during the 2022 IPO face further dilution, while the expanded free float could improve liquidity for international funds.
